intuition: Find a land cell that has not yet been counted, then visit all land connected to it. That whole group is one island. Mark cells as you visit them so the next scan does not count the group again. Only cells sharing a side connect; diagonal contact is not enough.

When an unvisited land cell is found, increment the count once and flood its entire component. The reference changes discovered land to water to record visitation without a separate boolean grid. Later scan positions therefore cannot start another flood for that same island.

Use a queue for the flood, considering only up, down, left, and right. Mark a neighbor immediately when it is enqueued, not later when it is removed. Otherwise two frontier cells could discover the same neighbor before either copy is processed, causing unnecessary repeated queue entries.

The reference deliberately mutates grid to reuse its storage for discovery marks. A caller that needs the original terrain can instead keep a set of visited coordinates or a boolean visited grid and leave the characters unchanged. That variant has the same O(rows*cols) time bound, with additional O(rows*cols) visitation storage.

steps: In the three-component fixture, rows are 11000, 11000, 00100, and 00011. Start scanning at (0,0).
The land at (0,0) starts island 1. Flood its neighbors (1,0), (0,1), and then (1,1), marking all four cells visited.
The scan later reaches (2,2), still land. It has no four-direction land neighbor, so it forms island 2 alone.
At (3,3), begin island 3. Its right neighbor (3,4) joins the same flood and cannot be counted separately.
The diagonal contact between (2,2) and (3,3) does not connect them. No unvisited land remains, so return 3.

codeNotes.note: Only remaining land can start a new component. Cells changed to water by earlier floods are deliberately skipped during the outer scan.
Each queue is a frontier for one newly counted island. Flooding finishes that component before the row-major scan resumes.
Marking before enqueueing guarantees each land cell is discovered once, even when several neighboring cells can reach it.

keyDecision: Count an island once at its first unvisited land cell. Mark neighbors before adding them to the queue.

concept.question: How does painting a whole connected patch count it only once?
intuition: Counting individual land squares overcounts islands. Even starting a separate traversal at every land square would recount patches that were already discovered.

When the scan finds unvisited land, count one new island and flood through all side-connected land from it. Mark the whole patch before scanning onward. Later squares in that patch are already accounted for.
concept.observation: Only shared sides connect land; diagonal contact does not join islands.
approach: Scan for an unvisited land square.
Count one island and mark all side-connected land in its flood.
Continue until every land square belongs to a counted flood.
concept.correctness: A flood reaches exactly the land connected to its starting square by side-sharing paths. Marking that component prevents any of its cells from starting another count. Every component contains a first unvisited cell in the scan, which starts one flood. Thus components and counted islands correspond one to one.

complexity.explanation: Each cell is scanned and each land square is flooded at most once, so work grows with grid area. The flood frontier can hold a grid-sized number of cells.

pitfalls: Only shared sides connect land; diagonal contact does not join islands.
Use four-direction adjacency, not diagonal adjacency.
